Krakatoa and the Sunda Strait.
The memory of the appalling catastrophe that in August 1883 struck the island of Krakatoa and the neighbouring coasts of Java and Sumatra
is—as always happens—effaced by the stream of later events and impressions.
Yet we may well suppose that it has not vanished altogether,
or the readers of our periodical will peruse with interest the following account by Mr Edmond Cotteau, who, by order of the French government,
a few months after the disaster visited the regions ravaged by the eruption and reported what he found.
Of the eruption itself none of those still living were witnesses; yet from the destruction it wrought
we may infer in some measure what spectacle the doomed island and the surrounding country must have offered on those terrible days of August.
We now give the floor to Mr Cotteau.
On 11 May 1884 I found myself, after a very interesting excursion to Sarawak (Borneo), at Singapore.
The Oxus, of the Compagnie des Messageries Maritimes, had just arrived; on board were my two friends,
Messrs Bréon and Korthals, with whom, on behalf of the Ministry of Public Instruction,
a scientific mission to the Sunda Strait and the volcanic island of Krakatoa had been entrusted.
I had left Paris a month earlier: we now met again at the appointed place.
On the evening of the same day we went aboard the steamer
which, twice a month after the arrival of the French mail, carries passengers and letters to Batavia,
where we arrived on 14 May, after a pleasant voyage of fifty-two hours.
As soon as we were comfortably settled, we took the steps necessary to ensure the success of the mission entrusted to us,
which could not be accomplished without help and cooperation from higher authority.
Fortunately everything went smoothly.
The Consul of France, Count de Pourtalès, was eager to serve us;
the Governor-General of the Dutch Indies, Mr van der Put, and the Director of the Royal Observatory at Batavia, Mr van Bemmelen,
placed themselves entirely at our disposal.
